items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: He wrote lyrics to some songs and was friendly with Eddie Condon and that bunch.

ctx.x: I see. The social club then was integrated?

To an extent yes. I mean, but the white people, you would see them there, like Joe Bushkin, would be musicians or people who were pretty hip. Like I think with Joe was Johnny DeVries, who was a sometime lyricist. He wrote lyrics to some songs and was friendly with Eddie Condon and that bunch. Lips would play — Eddie Condon’s had jam sessions like on Tuesday nights, not Mondays, but Tuesdays, and Lips was very often a guest there. Condon’s was one of the few places in the village that was — the band was…
Well you must have been on your way to becoming pretty hip yourself, even maybe you didn’t even realize it.

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Then Eddie Condon’s. I went there with Nat. That’s how I met Eddie, who was a wonderful person.

ctx.x: Actually, pre- – well, simultaneously with my budding friendship with Nat Lorber, I also – the first musician who – aside from this little incident with Tadd Dameron that I described – there were two musicians, both of whom were guys who were involved in proselytizing for jazz. The first one was Art Hodes. Art was – that was at Jimmy Ryan’s. Art was – he – we started talking. He wanted to know where I was from, and so on and so forth. He was very nice to me. That was around the same time at Ryan’s that I first…

afternoon sessions at a place – it was a hotel in mid-town Manhattan, but I can’t remember the name of it. It didn’t last very long. Wilbur also cultivated me. In other words, he was very nice to me and put me on his mailing list. Guys that I got chummy with – it was such a – you had such easy access to musicians. We didn’t – Nat and I, we never went inside Nick’s. We didn’t even want to go there, because we weren’t particularly interested in hearing the by-then not very interesting Dixieland that was being…

You said that, for example, you weren’t going to Nick’s too often, because the music wasn’t all that exciting. Were you shaping your own tastes at the time? Were they leaning in any particular – would you go to bebop and straight-ahead things?
